habitat: Atlantic Forest, tropical forests and agricultural areas
distribution: Southeast and South Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina
description: One of the most common venomous snakes in Brazil. It has brownish-gray coloration with dark triangular spots along its back. Responsible for most snakebite accidents in the country. Can reach up to 1.60m in length.
reproduction: Viviparous — gives birth to 12 to 18 offspring per litter
medicalImportance: High — hemotoxic venom that causes intense pain, swelling, hemorrhage and necrosis at the bite site
curiosity: Jararaca venom was fundamental for the development of Captopril, a medication used to control hypertension.

habitat: Cerrado, Caatinga and open areas of Brazil
distribution: All of Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, Argentina
description: Famous for the rattle at the end of its tail, made of keratin rings that produce a vibrating sound when the snake feels threatened. It has a robust body with brown coloration and dark diamond shapes on its back. Can reach up to 1.80m.
reproduction: Viviparous — gives birth to 15 to 30 offspring per litter
medicalImportance: Very high — neurotoxic venom that can cause respiratory paralysis, double vision and acute kidney failure
curiosity: The rattlesnake's rattle is made of keratin — the same material as our fingernails. Each skin shedding adds a new ring.

distribution: Southeast and South Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina
description: Has the most potent venom among Brazilian snakes and one of the most potent in the world. Characterized by colored rings — red, black and white — that run along its entire body. It is a small to medium-sized snake, rarely exceeding 1m. Despite its potent venom, it is docile and rarely attacks humans.
medicalImportance: Very high — neurotoxic venom that blocks nerve transmission, potentially leading to respiratory arrest within hours
curiosity: There are 'false coral snakes' that mimic the colored rings of the true coral. To tell them apart, observe: in the true coral, the rings complete the full circle around the body.

distribution: All of Brazil and South America
description: One of the largest Brazilian snakes, reaching up to 4m in length. It has no venom — it kills its prey by constriction, wrapping its body around the victim until breathing stops. It has brown coloration with characteristic dark geometric patterns.
reproduction: Viviparous — gives birth to 20 to 50 offspring per litter
medicalImportance: None — no venom; bite may cause only mechanical injury with no risk of death
curiosity: The boa has labial pits — small openings near the mouth that detect heat, allowing it to 'see' prey in the dark.

habitat: Rivers, lakes, swamps and flooded areas of the Amazon
distribution: North and Central-West Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia
description: The largest snake in Brazil and one of the largest in the world, exceeding 6m in length and weighing over 90kg. It is semi-aquatic, spending most of its time submerged with only its eyes and nostrils above water. It has no venom — it kills by constriction.
diet: Fish, aquatic birds, capybaras and even small caimans
reproduction: Viviparous — gives birth to 20 to 80 offspring per litter
medicalImportance: None — no venom; may cause bite injuries but is not lethal
curiosity: The anaconda's eyes and nostrils are on top of its head — a perfect adaptation to see and breathe while the rest of the body is submerged.

habitat: Dense tropical forests of the Amazon and Atlantic Forest
description: The largest venomous viper in South America, reaching up to 3m in length. It has rough scales that give a 'bristly' appearance. It is the only American viper that lays eggs. Its tail ends in a pointed scale that vibrates when threatened.
medicalImportance: Very high — hemotoxic and neurotoxic venom; accidents are rare (lives in remote areas) but often fatal without treatment
curiosity: The scientific name 'Lachesis muta' is a tribute to Lachesis, one of the three Fates in Greek mythology who measured the thread of life.

habitat: Fields, wetlands and open areas of Southern Brazil
description: Also known as 'cruzeira' in Southern Brazil. It has brown coloration with horseshoe-shaped patterns on the sides of its body. It is a robust snake that can reach 1.70m. Notoriously aggressive when cornered, it vibrates its tail and strikes quickly.
reproduction: Viviparous — gives birth to 13 to 25 offspring per litter
medicalImportance: High — hemotoxic venom with action similar to the jararaca, causing necrosis and hemorrhage
curiosity: The name 'urutu' comes from Tupi-Guarani and means 'snake that bites' — a direct description of its reputation among indigenous peoples.

distribution: All of Brazil, from Mexico to Argentina
description: One of the most agile and fastest snakes in Brazil, reaching 3m in length. It has shiny black coloration with yellow or orange bands. Despite having no venom, it is quite aggressive when cornered — it inflates its neck and strikes repeatedly.
diet: Rodents, birds, eggs and small reptiles
medicalImportance: None — no venom; bite may cause injury and secondary infection
curiosity: The tiger ratsnake is an excellent tree climber, able to climb vertical trunks with ease to hunt bird nests.

habitat: Forests, cerrado and dense vegetation areas
distribution: Southeast and South Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina
description: An extremely thin and elongated snake that perfectly camouflages among branches and vines. It can reach 2m in length but rarely exceeds 2cm in diameter. Green or brownish-green coloration. Completely harmless to humans — it flees at the slightest sign of danger.
diet: Amphibians, especially small frogs and tree frogs
medicalImportance: None — no venom and poses no risk to humans
curiosity: Its extremely thin and elongated body is a perfect evolutionary adaptation: it allows rapid movement among thin branches where larger predators cannot reach it.

distribution: All of Brazil, Mexico to Argentina
description: Known as 'the good snake' — it is immune to the venom of venomous snakes and feeds almost exclusively on them. It has glossy bluish-black coloration on its back and white or cream on its belly. It can reach 2.5m. It is an important natural controller of jararaca and rattlesnake populations.
diet: Venomous snakes (jararacas, rattlesnakes) and occasionally lizards and rodents
medicalImportance: None — no venom; on the contrary, it protects rural areas by reducing populations of venomous snakes
curiosity: The mussurana is so efficient at hunting jararacas that farmers used to keep them alive on their properties as natural 'biological control'.
